newsitem.title: UK: Belgian motives pondered as franc sneaks lower.
newsitem.headline: Belgian motives pondered as franc sneaks lower.

text.p: Often overlooked by players in the currency markets, the Belgian franc has tiptoed below its ERM midrate against the mark.

An insignificant blip in the big scheme of things, perhaps, but analysts said that if the franc's weakness continued, Belgium may surprise the markets with an interest rate rise. Others wondered if Belgium was actually quite content to see a softer franc.
"It may not be hugely significant, but it is a potential concern," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Banque Paribas in London.
"If the Belgian franc loses further ground it's possible the central bank may consider a unilateral shift in monetary policy. Exactly what level could prompt a move is anybody's guess."

Analysts draw a parallel with the Netherlands, where rates rose several times this year, as the guilder eased. The moves surprised traders who expect policymakers behind "satellite" mark currencies to follow meekly in the Bundesbank's footsteps.
"All of a sudden the Dutch were raising rates to protect the guilder which had slid down without gathering much attention," said Wattret. "The same could happen to the Belgian franc."

Some analysts said there was domestic justification for tightening in the Dutch economy, considered to be advanced in the economic cycle. But others say Belgium, although under no inflationary pressure, would be sensitive to a weaker franc.
While the market for francs is small, speculative interest has risen in the run-up to European monetary union. Belgium's repo market is one of Europe's most liquid.

"Interest has stepped up tremendously in the last three years," said Bank Brussels Lambert dealer Duncan Frost in London. "Before the turbulence in 1993 most banks didn't even have an ERM trading desk."
Pegged to the mark in 1990, and held within 0.5 percent of its central ERM rate by Belgium's central bank, the franc has remained stable through several bouts of European forex turmoil.

But in January this year, the mark rose above its ERM midrate of 20.6255 Belgian francs for the first time since May 1995. At the time, the 1995 weakness was put down to political twitchings but analysts said that argument no longer applies.
The franc has been drifting lower ever since, but so gently that its rock-solid reputation has not been rattled.
On Friday, the mark was at 20.65 Belgian francs, some five cents higher than at the start of the year.
The steady, if gradual, downtrend is puzzling economists.
The only action from the Belgian National Bank so far has been to drain off liquidity repeatedly through its daily repurchase agreements, pushing market rates higher.

One sketchy theory is that Belgium might not mind a soft franc -- which would please exporters -- as there are less than nine months before the European Monetary Institute (EMI) decides how to lock currencies into the euro. The EMI is keeping markets guessing but the consensus is that either current EMS midrates or a period average of bilateral rates will be used.

"Locking the franc into EMU (European Monetary Union) at a low rate would benefit growth in Belgium," said Frost. "However, Belgian policymakers are not the type to weaken their currency in order to boost growth."
But another trader at a Belgian Bank said: "As far as Europe goes we're in an era of relative deflation. Everybody wants weak currencies, and policymakers will grab any advantage they can."
EMU rates are of key concern to the project's mainstay, the mark, which has been battered by the dollar this year.

"We've got an anomaly where the mark is perceived as weak, but compared to some European crosses it's firmer," said Wattret of Paribas. "That held for the guilder earlier this year and is arguably the case for the Belgian franc now."
Frost of BBL said the franc could be suffering, like the mark, as a core member of what some think may be a weak euro.
The French franc was among core European units that slid against the mark recently, hit by dollar strength. In contrast, the Swiss franc and sterling are popular as safe-havens.
The Belgian franc aside, economists say ERM markets would be shaken up if dollar/mark breaches the 2.0 level.
"A rate rise in Germany would send everything haywire," said Frost. "It would almost certainly spark moves from Belgium and France, and Europe is just not ready for higher rates."
